verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a psalm to David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary: The superscription is part of the Hebrew verse count, which is why the KJV's 'verse 1' is our verse 2. Here, the title tells you three things. The song is handed to the choirmaster (מְנַצֵּחַ, from נצח, 'to excel, to lead'), so it was meant to be sung in the Temple and not only prayed in secret. It is a מִזְמוֹר, a piece sung to stringed accompaniment. And it is לְדָוִד, 'to/of David', where the preposition can mean authorship or dedication. Do not over-play the title: it carries no hint of a historical occasion. Radak and Meiri place the psalm in David's flight from Saul, and Malbim ties it to Doeg the Edomite, but the Hebrew names no circumstance. The KJV's 'chief Musician' is an acceptable guess for an uncertain office.

philological_notes.note: A participle with the preposition ל, from a root that means to be pre-eminent or to lead. It is a term of the temple singers' office; its exact sense (choirmaster, conductor, overseer) is uncertain. YLT renders it 'Overseer'.

verses.translation_literal: Hear, God, my voice in my complaint; from dread of an enemy you will guard my life.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear me, God. Hear my voice as it pours out its complaint. Fear of the enemy is on me like cold air, and only you can keep my life whole.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens as the sufferer's raw voice, and the actor should keep the first line close to speech: no preamble, no praise, just the imperative 'Hear.' The word שִׂיחַ is not 'prayer', as the KJV has it. It is murmuring, brooding talk, a complaint spoken out loud; Radak says it is the telling of troubles (סיפור התלאות), and the same word appears for the psalmist's restless speech in Psalm 55:3 (Meiri points to it). The KJV 'prayer' sands the edge off a word that means 'I am going on about it.' The second half is a puzzle that translators resolve in opposite ways. מִפַּחַד אוֹיֵב means 'from dread of an enemy' and 'fear of the enemy' is not the same: the dread is what the speaker feels, not the thing the enemy does to him. The verb תִּצֹּר is an imperfect, 'you will guard', and can be a prayer ('guard') or a confidence ('you guard'); YLT takes it as a statement. The Hebrew keeps the ambiguity, so the actor chooses: pleading, or already half-sure. The tradition collected in Rashi and Metzudat David reads the psalm as David's prophecy of Daniel in the lions' den, with the enemy being the satraps of Darius; that is the midrash, not the plain sense.

philological_notes.note: 'In my complaint, in my brooding speech'. Not a formal prayer (that would be תְּפִלָּה). Radak glosses it as the recounting of troubles; Meiri compares Psalm 55.
Dread, a shuddering fear. The phrase 'dread of an enemy' names the speaker's feeling, not what the enemy does.
'You will guard, keep'. An imperfect that can be read as a wish or a statement of trust. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as 'let my voice be heard so that you preserve my life'.

verses.translation_literal: You will hide me from the secret council of evildoers, from the tumult of workers of wickedness,
verses.translation_dramatic: Hide me. Hide me from the whispered council of men who mean harm, from the stir of a crowd that works wickedness.
verses.directors_commentary: Two words carry the whole scene, and they pull in opposite directions. סוֹד is a hushed council, a conspiracy behind closed doors; רִגְשָׁה is a noisy mob. The actor should make the listener hear both: whispering in a room, and then the same men shouting in a crowd. The KJV's 'insurrection' is too political, and the BBE's 'band' is too weak: the root רגשׁ is the one in Psalm 2:1, 'why do the nations rage?', and Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say so directly. It is the sound of a crowd getting loud, not a rebellion. Radak notes that סוֹד names the gathering itself, since the people who share a secret sit together and speak, and agreement comes out of the group as one voice. The word 'iniquity' in the KJV for אָוֶן is a safe churchy word; the Hebrew is closer to 'trouble-making, harm', and the workers of it are people whose job is mischief. The verb 'hide' (סתר) is the same one that will return in 'secret places' (verse 5); the protector's hiding and the attackers' hiding meet there.

philological_notes.note: A confidential council, a circle of people who plan together in secret. Radak says the word names the gathering, because those who share a secret sit together; Meiri keeps the plain sense of 'secret'.
The noise and bustle of a crowd. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link it to 'why do the nations rage' (Psalm 2:1); Radak glosses it simply as 'a multitude'.

verses.translation_literal: Who have sharpened their tongue like a sword, [who] have bent their arrow, a bitter word,
verses.translation_dramatic: They have whetted their tongues like swords. They have drawn the bow and set the arrow on the string, and the arrow is a bitter word.
verses.directors_commentary: The images should be played as physical actions. A sword needs a whetstone, so the tongue is rubbed on the stone until it will cut. An arrow needs a bow, and דָּרַךְ means to tread on it, to bend it with the foot and the weight of the body, as an archer strings a strong bow. The KJV's 'bend their bows to shoot their arrows' adds a bow to the Hebrew. The Hebrew says 'bent their arrow', where the bow is understood and the arrow is named, and the arrow itself is then identified: 'a bitter word'. The punch of the line is the last two words. The KJV's plural 'even bitter words' blurs the singular דָּבָר מָר, one bitter word, one thing in flight. In the ancient world, bitter (מַר) is also the taste of poison, and Malbim reads the verse as the poison smeared on the arrow, which gives the weapon a second reach: the sword kills close, the arrow from a distance, and the lie works both ways. Ibn Ezra notes that some read 'bitter word' as attached to the tongue or the deed.

philological_notes.note: 'They bent, trod' (the bow). The verb is used of drawing a bow by pressing it with the foot, hence the English 'bend'. The bow is implied and the arrow is the grammatical object.
'A bitter word', singular. Malbim takes 'bitter' as the poison on the arrow; Metzudat David makes it a charge meant to bring about death in the lions' den.

verses.translation_literal: To shoot in the hiding places [at] the innocent; suddenly they shoot him, and they do not fear.
verses.translation_dramatic: From their hiding places they shoot at the innocent. They shoot him suddenly, and they are not afraid.
verses.directors_commentary: This is an ambush, and it should be played quietly, like a held breath. The archers are in hiding, the target is unarmed, and the shot comes without warning. The Hebrew has a verb, יָרָה, that means to throw or cast and is used of archery; it sounds the same as the verb for fear, יָרֵא, in the last word, so listeners hear 'shoot' and 'fear' as near-twins: they shoot, and they do not fear. That play is lost in every English version, and the actor should lean on the repeated vowel and the flat 'not'. The target is תָּם, 'the innocent, the whole, the one without fault', where the KJV's 'the perfect' sounds like moral perfection. Nothing is claimed about sinlessness: the man is simply blameless in this quarrel, and Radak says it is David speaking of himself, one who went about in integrity and harmed none of them. The KJV 'shoot at him' hides the sudden switch from plural to singular: a gang against one man. Ibn Ezra hears the last clause as 'they do not fear the God who sees them', which is the theme of the next verse, and Meiri reads it so too.

philological_notes.note: 'Whole, blameless, without fault'. It does not mean flawless in the English sense of 'perfect', as the KJV and YLT have it. It is the term used of Job (Job 1:1).
'They shoot him'. The singular suffix after a plural verb sets one man against the group. Radak adds that an archer's victim does not guard against the shot he cannot see.

verses.translation_literal: They strengthen for themselves an evil word; they tell of hiding snares; they say, "Who will see them?"
verses.translation_dramatic: They put heart into one another over an evil plan. They talk over how to bury the traps. And they say, "Who will see them?"
verses.directors_commentary: The conspirators now speak for themselves. The second half of the verse turns from the archery of verse 4 to the world of the hunter: the מוֹקֵשׁ is a snare, a trap set in the ground and covered over, and 'to hide' (טמן) is what a trapper does to it. The verb יְחַזְּקוּ means to make strong, and Ibn Ezra reads it as mutual encouragement: this man strengthens that one to do evil. The KJV's 'encourage themselves' is right; what the audience should hear is a group of men talking each other into it. The verb יְסַפְּרוּ is 'they recount, they tell', a word more often used for telling stories, so the ambush is planned the way tales are shared, over a table. The closing question is the sin: מִי יִרְאֶה לָמוֹ, 'who will see them?' Radak and Meiri hear this as the denial that God sees. Play it flat and sure. The pronoun לָמוֹ is a poetic, archaic form of 'to them' and appears twice in this verse, and its cousin עָלֵימוֹ turns up in verse 9, a mark of high style and of a sinister chorus. The KJV 'privily' is a Tudor word for 'in secret' and means nothing to a modern ear.

philological_notes.note: Snares, traps for birds or animals, a common figure in the Psalms for the plots of enemies. The word is plural.
'They make strong'. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'one makes the other strong to do evil'; Radak reads it as strengthening their charge against David with forceful pleas.
A poetic form of 'to them', an extended form of ל with the suffix. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'to them' (להם).

verses.translation_literal: They search out injustices; they have completed a search searched out; and the inward part of a man, and a heart, [is] deep.
verses.translation_dramatic: They search, and what they search for is wrong. They comb and comb, hunting for a crack to pour their malice into. And the search is done; every corner has been turned. Whatever any of them knows, he keeps it down in the dark, for the inside of a person is a well without a bottom, and the heart goes deeper still.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is a knot of one root. The verb 'search out' (yachpesu), the noun 'search' (chefes) and the passive participle 'searched out' (mechupas) all come from chafas, so the line sounds like a hand turning over a room: they search, a search, a searched-out search. English cannot repeat the sound without strain, which is why the literal layer repeats the word. KJV 'a diligent search' makes it respectable, almost scholarly. The Hebrew keeps the sense of rummaging, and what is rummaged for is 'olot, injustices or false charges. Rashi glosses it as pretexts and quotes Daniel 6:5, where the court officials 'sought to find a ground of complaint', so the world of this verse is the accusation brought to a ruler, not a street brawl. Be aware of the reading that changes the voice. The form tamnu is, in the ancient commentators (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion), a variant of tammu, 'they have completed', with the nun standing for the doubled letter; they compare Lamentations 3:22. On that reading the whole verse is narration: they complete the search they had searched. YLT and ASV prefer 'we', the plotters' own boast, 'We have perfected a searching search', and ASV even adds 'say they', which the Hebrew does not have. Both are possible, and nothing in the Hebrew marks the speech; play it as narration and let the cast decide if it wants the boast. The last clause closes the thought. 'Inward part' (qerev) is the guts, and 'heart' (lev) is the place of thinking; the pair is the whole hidden person. 'Deep' is the plotters' own confidence in their secrecy, as in the previous verse, 'Who will see them?'. KJV 'of every one of them' puts words in that the Hebrew does not use; it says 'a man'.

philological_notes.note: 'Search out', 'rummage'. The root occurs three times in the line (verb, noun chefes, participle mechupas), a sound-play that gives the sense of a thorough, intensive search; STEPBible 'they plot' is a gloss from the context, not the root's meaning.

Read by the commentators as a form of tammu, 'they have completed', with the nun in place of the doubled letter, third person: 'they have completed a search searched out'. The other reading takes it as first person plural, 'we have finished', the plotters' own boast (YLT, ASV). The literal layer follows the commentators.
'Injustices', plural, here used for the false charges they look for or devise. Rashi glosses it as pretexts, citing Daniel 6:5.

verses.translation_literal: And God shot them, an arrow, suddenly; they have become their wounds.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then God shoots. One arrow, from nowhere, and nothing was ever said about the sound of it. The ones who aimed in the dark are struck before they know the bow was drawn. Their wounds are all that is left of them, and the wounds are their own.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn of the psalm is one short line. For the whole psalm the enemies have been the archers, who 'shoot in secret places' and whose tongues are sharpened like swords (v. 4-5). Now God is the archer, and the same verb of shooting is used, with the same word for suddenly. Take care here: 'suddenly' is the word of v. 5, where they shoot at the innocent. It is the same adverb, spelled defectively there (פִּתְאֹם) and with a full vav here (פִּתְאוֹם), both with alef; the two spellings are one word. The reversal is meant to be heard. The grammar is a puzzle for translators. The verb is a vav-consecutive form, normally narrative past, 'and God shot them'. Radak and Meiri say the prophets often put the past where we expect the future, a confident certainty; KJV, ASV and Webster have 'shall shoot', BBE 'sends' and YLT 'doth shoot'. Rashi and Metzudat David instead read it as a past event and tie it to Daniel in the den of lions (Daniel 6:25). The staging follows the Hebrew: God has already shot. The second clause has no verb meaning 'wounded'. It says 'they have become their wounds', a noun sentence in which the people are replaced by what has been done to them; KJV 'shall they be wounded' flattens that into plain passive grammar. Malbim sees the traps they set for David turning into their own wound, the plotters hit by their own plan. The arrow is not an ordinary weapon here. In the ancient Near East divine arrows are plague, lightning and sudden death, and the line promises that what the wicked do secretly God does openly, with exactly the same tool.

philological_notes.note: 'Suddenly'. The same adverb as פִּתְאֹם in v. 5, there written defectively and here with a full vav. The repetition marks the reversal: those who shot 'suddenly' at the innocent are shot 'suddenly' by God.

'And he shot them', vav-consecutive imperfect with the object suffix 'them'. Radak and Meiri read the past as standing for the future, in the manner of prophecy; Rashi and Metzudat David take it as a past event.

verses.translation_literal: And they made him stumble, upon them their tongue; all who see them shake [the head].
verses.translation_dramatic: Their own tongue trips them, and the fall is theirs. Everyone who sees them shakes with it.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the most tangled verse in the psalm, and the English versions disagree sharply. Start with the verb: וַיַּכְשִׁילוּהוּ is plural, 'and they made him stumble', with a singular 'him' that has no clear antecedent. Radak and Meiri say the 'him' is the tongue, and Meiri compares other Hebrew passages where a plural verb takes a singular suffix. So the sense is: their tongue, which they sharpened against the victim in verse 4, now falls on them, and they are the ones who stumble. The KJV's 'they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves' gets the sense right but puts the grammar in the future and makes the tongue the thing that falls. The weapon is thrown back at the thrower. The last clause hinges on יִתְנֹדְדוּ, from נדד, 'to wander, flee, shake'. The KJV 'flee away' takes the sense of flight; the ASV 'wag the head' follows Rashi and Metzudat David, who read it as mocking head-shaking. A reader of the first audience would hear both a shudder and a retreat. The actor should play the onlookers as stunned, and not as gloating: the crowd shakes its head at a spectacle it did not expect. Malbim sees a measure-for-measure justice in the line: the lie that was meant to snare the victim snared the liar.

philological_notes.note: 'And they made him stumble'. Radak and Meiri take the singular suffix as pointing to the tongue. The hif'il of כשל is used for causing someone to fall.
A hitpael of נדד, 'wander, flee, shake'. The senses are flight (KJV 'flee away') and head-shaking (ASV 'wag the head'; Rashi, Metzudat David). Meiri glosses it as trembling from the uproar.

verses.translation_literal: And all humankind feared, and they declared the deed of God, and his work they understood.
verses.translation_dramatic: And all mankind is afraid. They tell what God has done, and they take in his work and understand it.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now widens from the plotters' circle to all of humankind, and the verbs move into a chain of 'and': they feared, they declared, they understood. The KJV 'for they shall wisely consider' invents a causal 'for' where the Hebrew has only 'and', and puts the whole verse into the future. In the Hebrew the sequence is a story told in order: fear first, then speech, then understanding. The fear is the right fear (the root ירא is the one that the plotters lacked in verse 5, 'and they do not fear'), so the audience sees the missing fear restored in the crowd. Ibn Ezra says the fear comes when people see God repay the wicked according to their own plans. The verb הִשְׂכִּילוּ comes from שׂכל, 'to have insight, to see the point', and is the same as the word in the headings of the 'maskil' psalms: the onlookers do not merely see an event, they read it. Malbim adds that the effect is to teach that there is providence and judgment. Note פֹּעַל אֱלֹהִים, 'the deed of God': the plotters were פֹּעֲלֵי אָוֶן, 'workers of wickedness' in verse 3, and now God has a deed, using the same root, פעל. The workers have their work answered by the work of God.

philological_notes.note: 'They understood, they gained insight'. The hif'il of שׂכל means to grasp something intelligently. Radak says it means they understand that God is judge and watches over the world.
'The deed of God'. The root פעל is the same as in 'workers (פֹּעֲלֵי) of wickedness' in verse 3, so the wicked workers are matched by the deed of God.

verses.translation_literal: The righteous will rejoice in YHWH and will take refuge in him; and all upright of heart will boast.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the righteous man will rejoice in the LORD. He will run to him and find shelter there. And all those whose hearts are straight will lift up their voices and boast of him.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends in the opposite key to its opening. It began with a voice that complained in fear, and it closes with gladness. KJV 'shall be glad ... and shall trust' is accurate in sense but smooths two matters. First, the verb. 'Will rejoice' (yismach) is an imperfect that can also be read as a wish, 'let the righteous rejoice', which is how STEPBible glosses it; the next verb, vechasa, is a vav-perfect that continues the first rather than starting a new wish, so the line either wishes or predicts as a whole. The staging follows the prediction: the line comes after God's act, so the gladness is the result. Radak even makes the vav of 'and he takes refuge' mean 'when', 'because he has seen the vengeance on his enemies'. Second, 'trust' for chasa loses the picture. The root is to seek shelter, as under a rock or a wing; 'take refuge' (ASV) keeps it. The last verb, yithallelu, is the reflexive of 'praise', and its sense is to boast, to praise oneself in someone, so 'glory' (KJV) is right in effect but now archaic, and BBE's 'give him glory' changes the direction: they glory in God, not give glory to him. Rashi even says the upright boast of their own uprightness, sure that God is their help. Rashi names the righteous man Daniel, and Meiri reports both that midrash and the plain sense, that David speaks of himself. 'Upright of heart' closes the frame with the heart from the earlier verses: the plotters had a deep heart for hiding, and these have a straight one.

philological_notes.note: Imperfect, 'he will rejoice', which can be read as a wish, 'let him rejoice' (STEPBible). The following וְחָסָה is a vav-perfect continuing it. The literal layer reads the line as prediction.
'And will take refuge', the idea of seeking shelter. Radak reads the vav as 'when' or 'because', tying the refuge to seeing God's vengeance.

Reflexive of 'praise': 'boast, glory in'. STEPBible gives 'let them boast'; here it is a plain imperfect, 'will boast'. Rashi says the upright boast in their own uprightness; Metzudat David says they praise themselves for knowing that the LORD is God.
